sec.title: Study Objectives
sec.p: We evaluated the efficacy of a digitally delivered, small and scalable incentive-based intervention program on sleep and wellbeing in short-sleeping, working adults.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A 22-week, parallel-group, randomized-controlled trial was conducted on 21–40 y participants gifted with FitbitTM devices to measure sleep for ≥2 years, as part of a broader healthy lifestyle study. About 225 short sleepers (141 males; average time-in-bed, TIB < 7h) were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to Goal-Setting or Control groups. The Goal-Setting group received health vouchers (~USD 0.24) for meeting each sleep goal (i.e. increasing weeknight TIB by 30 min/sleeping before midnight).The study spanned three phases: (1) 2-week Baseline, (2) 10-week Intervention, and (3) 10-week Follow-Up. Wellbeing questionnaires were administered on Weeks 1–2, 11–12, and 21–22.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Baseline weeknight TIB (mean ± SD) was 387 ± 43 min (Goal-Setting) and 399 ± 44 min (Control), while bedtime was 00:53 ± 01:13 (Goal-Setting), and 00:38 ± 00:56 (Control). No difference in sleep outcomes was observed at study endpoints, but exploratory week-by-week analysis showed that on Weeks 3–5, TIB in the Goal-Setting group increased (9–18 min; ps < 0.05) while on Week 5, bedtimes shifted earlier (15 min; p < 0.01) compared to Baseline. Morning sleepiness was reduced in the Goal-Setting group (mean[SEM] = −3.17(1.53); p = 0.04) compared to Baseline, although between-group differences were not significant (p = 0.62). Main barriers to sleeping longer were work hours (35%), followed by leisure activities (23%) and family commitments (22%).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our program resulted in encouraging subjective sleep improvements and short-term sleep extension, but sustained transformation of sleep will probably require structural measures to overcome significant obstacles to sleep.

boxed-text.p: Insufficient sleep is prevalent among working adults, with short- and long-term consequences on health, wellbeing, and productivity. We combined small incentives with digital content delivery, goal-setting, and objective tracking to explore their effect on sleep and wellbeing in working adults with short sleep. We observed only transient improvements (~3 weeks) in sleep duration and bedtimes in participants who received incentives to sleep longer and before midnight. Despite this, most participants reported benefits from increased awareness into the importance of sleep. Barriers to sleeping longer were work hours, leisure activities, and family commitments. These underscore the importance of structural changes to support sleep promotion initiatives.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sleep is a key component to a healthy lifestyle and its deficiency has negative health and economic consequences [1,2]. However, many working adults curtail sleep for work, social, and leisure reasons. American workers average just 6.7–7.6 h of sleep on workdays [3], while in Singapore, about 66% of working adults reported sleeping less than 7 h a night [4]. As insufficient sleep is associated with impaired cognition, poorer relationships at work, increased absenteeism and reduced presenteeism, higher risk of traffic and work-related accidents, as well as increased long-term disease and economic burden [1,2,5,6], there is a compelling case to improve existing sleep habits.

Sleep promotion efforts that merely depend on sleep education/hygiene recommendations (e.g. avoiding caffeine close to bedtime and sleeping adequately at regular timings) are inexpensive and easily scalable, but have generally not garnered much success [7–9]. Adherence to stated intentions is often poor as a result of perceived lack of time or societal support, work- or family-related commitments, low motivation/readiness to change and unengaging content/mode of delivery/lack of feedback [10,11].

In a meta-analysis of behavioral sleep extension studies, Baron et al. found that direct intervention through prescription of a sleep schedule had the largest potential to increase sleep in the short-term, as compared to indirect methods like coaching/education [12]. They also found that studies which employed behavioral change tools (e.g. goal-setting, self-monitoring) produced more change. In addition, studies that used objective measures also evidenced larger effect sizes, perhaps due to provision of feedback or greater participant awareness of being monitored.

Alongside the increased adoption of consumer sleep trackers has been an expansion of digital/mHealth (mobile health) interventions. These could be used to deliver sleep education, goal-setting, engagement prompts, and objective tracking altogether on a single platform. mHealth apps can be effective for improving sleep (Cohen’s d = 0.87), although to date, improvements have been reported primarily in terms of subjective sleep quality [13].

The provision of incentives to encourage change in health behavior has had some success in physical activity [14] and weight loss [15]programs. Incentives can be financial [16,17] or in-kind (e.g. e-badges [18] and game rewards [19]). Incentives-based interventions have only recently been used to improve sleep. Scullin et al. launched an “8h sleep challenge”, where undergraduate students could earn extra credit to obtain at least 8 h of sleep for five nights leading up to a project deadline. About 22 students who took up the challenge managed to sleep an average of 98 min more each night than nonincentivized students enrolled in the same program, with no detriment to project performance [20]. In a separate study, Avery et al. used monetary incentives in college students across a 3-week period and increased the likelihood of sleeping 7–9 h by 19%, with some evidence of sustained change after 3 months [21]. Finally, in a randomized-controlled trial of 452 low-income workers over a 1-month period, participants who received financial incentives increased time in bed by 50 min compared to a control group [22]. Notably, all of these interventions have been<1 month in duration and did not specifically target those with short sleep. In addition, the incentives afforded were quite substantial (~USD1-6/night) and would not be cost-effective when scaled to a large population health study over a longer period.

The aim of the present study was to evaluate an intervention that combined features of successful strategies previously engaged in sleep intervention studies, i.e. establishing personalized sleep goals, rewarding goal attainment, and providing for objective self-monitoring of sleep. However, for this public health initiative to be sustainable, incentives could not be too large, but still sizable relative to levels participants were already receiving as part of a broader health monitoring study. Provision of too large incentives could also undermine building of intrinsic/autonomous motivation, a key component of long-term behavior change [23] and shifting of attitudes toward sleep [24]. Incentives here were instead framed as an encouragement/nudge to help participants improve their longer-term health and wellbeing.

The program was selectively delivered to habitually short-sleeping (<7 h TIB) working adults who were rewarded if they achieved personalized weeknight sleep duration and bedtime goals over a 10-week period. We anticipated that greater improvements would be observed in the Goal-Setting compared to the Control group that did not receive these goal-directed rewards. We also investigated if the program would initiate sustained behavioral change and/or benefits to subjective wellbeing following reward cessation.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This parallel-group, randomized-controlled trial was a sub-study of the “Health Insights Singapore” (hiSG) study, a longitudinal population health study initiated by the Health Promotion Board, Singapore in 2019. The first cohort comprised of 1951 young working adults aged 21–40 years who were given a device (Fitbit Ionic, Fitbit Inc, San Francisco, CA) to log their activity/sleep patterns over a 2-year period. Participants also installed a mobile application to complete surveys and were rewarded with Healthpoints convertible to vouchers if they wore the device, logged sleep and meals regularly, and completed surveys on the application. Furthermore, they were allowed to keep the device if they met study requirements over the 2-year period. Demographic, health, and lifestyle questionnaires were also obtained at study commencement. Upon completion of the initial 2-year period, participants were invited to renew their participation for a further 2 years.

Participants who were found to be short sleepers (average time-in-bed; TIB < 7 h) during the initial 2-year observational period were invited for a sleep intervention study termed the Health Insights Singapore—Sleep Health Study (hiSG-SHS). Study eligibility was determined during a 3-month pre-study period (Dec 2020–Feb 2021)—chosen as it was close to the intervention start date, and minimally affected by COVID-19 pandemic restriction measures known to affect sleep habits [25,26]. Additionally, shift workers, pregnant, or nursing mothers were excluded because they were expected to have irregular sleep schedules often beyond personal control. Of the 1500 participants who opted to renew participation in the original hiSG study, 432 met criteria for the sub-study, and 225 consented to take part (Figure 1). Participants were also provided with a new study device (Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Inc, San Francisco, CA), but sleep tracking capabilities remained similar to the previous device. This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04878380. The National Healthcare Group Domain Specific Review Board approved the study protocol. Informed consent was obtained from all subjects prior to study participation. Interim analyses were conducted at the end of Baseline and Intervention phases for evaluation of data quality, but no stopping guidelines were implemented and the trial continued to completion.

sec.title: Randomization and masking
sec.p: Participants who consented were randomly assigned to one of two groups, namely Goal-Setting (who were incentivised for reaching certain sleep goals) or Control (who were credited to simply log their sleep via the Fitbit tracker), in a 2:1 ratio [27], stratified by sex due to the higher prevalence of males with short sleep in our sample. Randomization was thus performed on every block of three male/female participants using a computer-generated assignment schedule, resulting in 150 (94 male) and 75 (47 male) participants in the Goal-Setting and Control groups respectively. About 25 participants also shared an address with at least 1 other participant; for these, they were randomized as a household unit (12 unique households). Randomization was conducted only after all participants had consented, and the random allocation sequence for group assignment was generated by researchers not involved in participant enrollment/study implementation.

Participants could not be blinded to their group assignment due to the nature of the study [14], and were aware of both study arms at the informed consent stage. However, analyses and participant communication were strictly handled by separate teams. Each participant was also first assigned an anonymized subject ID number. A computer-generated random allocation sequence was then used to group participants into either the Control or Goal-Setting group. In this way, no study staff was involved in the selection process. Finally, participants were only notified of their group assignment after the Baseline phase to prevent introduction of bias due to awareness of their assignment.

Power analyses indicated a sample of this size would be sensitive to a group difference in TIB of ≥ 10 min (using a pooled SD of 25 min based on pre-study TIB values). Such a gain would represent a meaningful increase, and similar to previous sleep intervention studies that were conducted over a shorter duration [21]. While our intention was to recruit 200 and 100 participants in the Goal-Setting and Control groups respectively to prevent a reduction in statistical power due to attrition, we were not able to garner sufficient interest from the remaining eligible participants. Nonetheless, only one male participant in the Goal-Setting group had to be dropped from the study due to technical issues; this participant had manually entered Fitbit sleep logs.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: The study was conducted over 22-weeks (August 15, 2021–January 14, 2022), split into three phases: (1) Baseline (Week 1–2), (2) 10-week Intervention (Week 3–12), and (3) 10-week Follow-Up (Week 13–22) (Figure 2).

Following a 2-week recruitment and informed consent period, participants in both groups completed 2 weeks of sleep logging and questionnaires (detailed below) during the Baseline phase (Week 1–2) (Figure 2). At the beginning of Week 3, both groups received a set of sleep hygiene tips (e.g. by going to bed earlier and at regular timings, winding down before bedtime, ensuring a conducive sleeping environment, removing electronic devices from the bedroom 30 min before sleep, avoiding large meals/alcohol/caffeine close to bedtime, and exercise as long as it was not at the expense of sleep). To instill intrinsic motivation and sense of agency, both groups also completed a self-reflection questionnaire surveying five areas of life that were most important to them (e.g. family, career, health, financial wealth, and physical fitness), and how they thought better sleep could help them in these areas.

During the Intervention phase (Week 3–12), participants in the Goal-Setting group were offered 50 Healthpoints (SGD $0.33/USD $0.24; 150 Healthpoints = SGD 1 ~ USD 0.72) per weeknight, for each of two objectives they met. These were (1) to sleep before midnight and (2) to clock 30 min more TIB above their pre-study TIB. We chose to base the sleep duration goal on a target that could be reasonably achieved, rather than on a standardized goal (e.g. 7 h). Bedtime and TIB were used as objectives as these sleep parameters are more likely to be within participants’ control. Waketime is largely determined by work start time and is often fixed for a given individual, while there is latitude to shift bedtime earlier. We avoided setting total sleep time (TST) as a goal as this might interfere with sleep initiation through creation of anxiety about sleep performance [28]. Reminders to log sleep, complete questionnaires, and sleep tips were again issued via the phone app at the end of each Intervention (Week 11–12) and Follow-Up (Week 21–22) phase.

Healthpoints were credited to participants’ accounts bi-weekly. Throughout the entire study period, participants in both groups were also rewarded with 20 Healthpoints per sleep log. In addition, if they logged a minimum of 3 weeknights (i.e. sleep periods commencing Sunday–Thursday night) per week, they would receive an additional 50 Healthpoints for that week. Questionnaires were also pushed through in-app surveys on Weeks 1–2, 11–12, and 21–22, for a maximum total of 2440 Healthpoints. These included once-per-phase surveys (i.e. the Sleep Health Index [29], Oldenburg Burnout Inventory [30], revised version of the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CESD-R) [31], as well as daily ecological momentary assessments (EMA) probing sleep quality (1—Very Poor to 5—Very Good), mood (0—Negative to 100—Positive), motivation, stress levels, and sleepiness (0—Not at all to 100—Extremely Likely) and work location (Home/Office/No Work) for that day, which were administered between 8 am and 12 pm of the morning following each sleep period during those 6 weeks. An exit survey was also administered at the end of the study to obtain qualitative feedback on study experiences and efficacy. Participants were asked if they (1) actively tried to change their sleep habits (“yes”, “no”) and (2) benefited from the program (open-ended response detailing benefits obtained or reasons for lack of benefits). Participants in the Goal-Setting group were additionally questioned whether or not they were regularly able to meet their sleep duration and bedtime goals (“yes”, “no”), as well to describe obstacles to achieving these goals (check all that apply from the categories: “Work hours”, “Family commitments”, Social commitments”, Leisure activities”, “Exercise activities”).

A detailed breakdown of Healthpoints awarded for each completed study component is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Meeting bedtime (+50 Healthpoints) and sleep duration (+50 Healthpoints) goals alone would reward a Goal-Setting participant with an additional 5000 Healthpoints (~SGD 33/USD 24) over the 10-week Intervention Phase.

sec.title: Fitbit sleep data pre-processing
sec.p: Only nocturnal sleep periods were considered, as these would be more easily modifiable in this working adult cohort. As a result of some participants having multiple nocturnal sleep episodes over a 24 h period (7% of data), sleep episodes had to meet the following criteria for inclusion in final analyses: (1) multiple sessions with bedtimes of 8 pm or later and before 12 noon the next day were combined into one session, unless the sleep period started at 8 am or later and ended at 12 noon or later. (2) Any sleep session (after combination of eligible sleep sessions in (1) that were <3h were excluded. For combined sleep sessions, bedtime was taken to be the earliest bedtime of all sleep sessions, TIB was defined from the start from the earliest bedtime to the latest waketime, while TST was taken to be the sum of all sleep epochs within that TIB period.

In accordance with our prior work on the original hiSG dataset [26], data were also filtered to remove days when participants did not wear the Fitbit for at least 8 h/day or when atypical activity levels were observed. The latter refers to records with (1) total daily steps > 50,000 and records with (2) no resting heart rate or (3) no recorded steps.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Primary sleep outcomes for the study were changes from Baseline for variables directly affected by the intervention (i.e. Fitbit-derived weekday TIB and bedtime), during the final two weeks of Intervention (Week 11–12) and Follow-Up (Week 21–22) phases. Secondary sleep outcomes analyzed were changes in proportion of days/week TIB and bedtime goals were met, weekday TST, wake time, sleep extension (weekend–weekday TIB), weekly TIB and bedtime variability (standard deviation of TIB and bedtime), social jetlag (weekend–weekday sleep midpoint) from the Fitbit, as well as changes in self-reported sleep health (duration, quality and disorder dimensions) from the Sleep Health Index, and changes in sleep quality from the EMA component.
We also assessed changes in wellbeing outcomes for overall burnout and depression, as well as changes to morning mood, motivation, stress levels, and sleepiness from the EMA component.

For each participant, a minimum of 3 weekdays/week for Fitbit and EMA logs across all endpoint weeks (Baseline, Intervention, Follow-Up) were required for inclusion in the final analysis, based on our earlier work that found this number to be sufficient for reliable sleep estimates [32], with the exception of TIB and bedtime variability, where a minimum of 5 days/week was required. This number was then averaged to obtain one value per phase for subsequent analyses. As there was a public holiday in the second week of the Intervention phase, this day was removed from all analyses.

Although the main study endpoints were sleep and wellbeing changes from Baseline on Weeks 11–12 (Intervention) and Weeks 21–22 (Follow-Up), exploratory analyses on changes in TIB and bedtime for all study weeks were conducted to probe changes that could occur throughout the study.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Analyses were conducted using SPSS version 27 (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). Independent samples t-tests (continuous variables) and chi-square tests (categorical variables) were used to determine differences in baseline characteristics between the Goal-Setting and Control groups.

To compare differences from Baseline between the Goal-Setting and Control groups at the main study endpoints (Week 11–12; Intervention) and (Week 21–22; Follow-Up), two (Group) by three (Phase) linear mixed-effects models were conducted using an unstructured covariance matrix to account for covariance of the residuals across the three phases. Participants nested within households were additionally modeled as a random effect, but as this did not improve model fit, we did not include this in the final analyses. Mixed models were utilized due to missing values in the sample, as this was found to be most powerful for longitudinal trials with missing values [33]. In addition, pairwise contrasts were used to test for significant differences between outcomes in each study phase (Intervention, Follow-Up) vs. Baseline and between groups (Goal-Setting vs. Control). Due to fluctuating work arrangements caused by COVID-19 movement restrictions during the study period, separate control analyses accounting for work location as an additional factor in the mixed-effects models were also conducted.

Finally, to examine week-by-week changes in sleep goals (TIB/bedtime) throughout the study period, paired t-tests were conducted on participants who contributed to the week of interest (Week 3–22) vs. outcomes in the Baseline phase (Week1–2; Figure 3).

Red and blue asterisks denote significant differences from baseline for the Control and Goal-Setting groups respectively. Black asterisks denote significant differences between groups.

sec.p: For all statistical tests, p-values of less than 0.05 were considered significant.

sec.title: Exit survey analysis
sec.p: Open-ended responses regarding benefits obtained from the study were further hand-coded by a single rater and reviewed by a second to indicate experienced benefit (“yes”), no benefit (“no”), or mixed benefits (“somewhat”). Detailed explanations were also categorized into one of five categories, based on the type of benefit experienced (“established change”, “tried to change”, “gained awareness”, “gained specific insights”, and “felt motivated”), and reasons for lack of benefits (“hard to break habits”, “too busy”, “too low incentives”, and “others”). Ambiguous responses were omitted from analysis.
Chi-square tests were used to determine differences in categorical exit survey outcomes between the Goal-Setting and Control groups.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The final sample comprised of 224 participants (Goal-Setting: 149, Control: 75). One participant from the Goal-Setting group had to be removed as this participant had manually entered Fitbit sleep logs. Across the 22-week study period (August 15, 2021–January 14, 2022), 20,057 weeknights and 7902 weekend Fitbit-derived sleep logs were collected out of a possible 34,272 nights (excluding 1 public holiday during the Intervention period). This was equivalent to a compliance rate of ~82% across the 22-week study period. About 211 participants (Goal-Setting: 140, Control: 71) provided valid Fitbit data (3 days/week across both weeks) in at least one study endpoint. For EMA, compliance was at 54% across all three phases, with 156 participants (Goal-Setting: 108, Control: 48) providing sufficient data (3 days/week across both weeks) in at least one study endpoint for consideration in the final EMA analyses. For the exit survey, 198 participants (Goal-Setting: 132, Control: 66) provided responses to the questionnaires provided.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics
sec.p: Groups did not significantly differ in demographic characteristics, baseline sleep, and wellbeing measures, number of Fitbit records, or daily Fitbit wear time (p’s > 0.05, Table 1). Baseline TIB (M ± SD) on weeknights was 399 ± 44 min (Control) and 387 ± 43 min (Goal-Setting), respectively, while Baseline bedtime on weeknights was 00:38 ± 00:56 (Control) and 00:53 ± 01:13 (Goal-Setting), indicating less than optimal TIB and bedtimes in this sample.

sec.p: Subjectively reported sleep health measures in our sample for the duration dimension were about five points below published US norms [29]. This was likely because we selected persons with relatively short sleep. Scores on the sleep quality and disorders dimensions were higher than United States, suggesting that our sample was otherwise healthy. Subjective sleep quality ratings assessed by EMA reports averaged between “Fair” and “Good”.

For wellbeing measures, participants reported “medium” burnout levels [34], and depression scores below the accepted cut-off (<16) for clinical depression (CESD-R). Mood and motivation scores were generally fair, at 67.6 and 59.8 points (out of 100), respectively while stress and sleepiness scores were at 28.3 and 31.2 points (out of 100), respectively, indicating modest levels of stress and sleepiness.

sec.title: Effect of intervention on sleep
sec.p: There were no between-group differences for the number of Fitbit records logged or daily wear time at the Intervention (Week 11–12) and Follow-Up (Week 21–22) end points (Intervention: 7.6 ± 2.1 (Goal-Setting) vs. 7.8 ± 1.9 (Control) records; 1229 ± 220 (Goal-Setting) vs. 1232 ± 191 (Control) min daily wear time; Follow-Up: 7.8 ± 2.6 (Goal-Setting) vs. 8.4 ± 2.4 (Control) records; 1224 ± 206 (Goal-Setting) vs. 1278 ± 153 (Control) min daily wear time).

Marginal means for each outcome as a function of Group (Goal-Setting and Control) and Phase (Baseline, Intervention and Follow-Up) are presented in Table 2. No significant Group × Phase interactions were found for any of the primary or secondary sleep outcomes (Table 2). For planned contrasts with Baseline outcomes, only the Sleep Health Index (duration dimension) was significantly increased in the Goal-Setting but not Control group (Goal-Setting: mean(SEM); 4.87(1.50) points; p = 0.001, Control: 1.26(2.06) points; p = 0.54), indicating increased subjectively perceived sleep. However, these changes from Baseline were not significantly different between groups (3.61(2.55) points; p = 0.16).

sec.p: As this study was performed from August 2021 to January 2022, during the COVID-19 pandemic, sleep habits may have been affected by hybrid working arrangements [35]. EMA measured day-by-day work location (at-home vs. in-person) did significantly influence sleep outcomes (p < 0.001)—with working from the office being associated with 25 min less TIB than working from home and much earlier wake than bedtimes. However, controlling for work location did not significantly alter the pattern of results observed.

To examine whether the intervention had an effect at any time during the intervention period (not just during the final 2-week endpoint), an exploratory week-by-week analysis was performed. When primary sleep outcomes were analyzed by week, significantly increased TIB (9–18 min; ps < 0.05) and earlier bedtimes (15 min; p < 0.01) compared to Baseline were observed only in the Goal-Setting group shortly after the intervention started (i.e. Weeks 3–5 for TIB, Week 5 for Bedtime; Figure 3). Between-group differences were significant only for Bedtime on Weeks 3, 4, and 6 (ps < 0.05; Figure 3). However, these gains in sleep were not sustained throughout the full duration of the intervention. A similar trend was observed in terms of proportion of days goals were met (Supplementary Figure S1). There was also a tendency towards longer TIB along with delayed bedtimes in both groups during the Follow-Up period (Weeks 17 and 20).

sec.title: Intervention effect on wellbeing outcomes
sec.p: Marginal means for each outcome as a function of group (Goal-Setting, Control) and phase (Baseline, Intervention and Follow-Up) are presented in Table 3. Although significant Group × Phase interactions were observed for burnout levels (p = 0.04) and morning stress (p = 0.02), underlying within-group changes were not significantly different from Baseline in both groups (ps > 0.07). For planned contrasts with Baseline outcomes, morning sleepiness measured by the EMA during the Intervention Phase was lower in the Goal-Setting but not Control group (Goal-Setting: −3.17(1.53) points; p = 0.04, Control: −1.89(2.11) points; p = 0.37). There was also a reduction in depression scores on average in the Goal-Setting group during the Follow-Up phase (−2.10(0.68); p = 0.002). However, both these within-group reductions were not significant between groups (ps > 0.17).

sec.title: Exit questionnaire
sec.p: Qualitative survey results are shown in Supplementary Figures S2 and S3. Slightly over half of the participants in both groups indicated that they actively tried to change their sleep habits, but no proportional differences between groups were observed (Goal-Setting vs. Control: 58% vs. 53%; p = 0.54; Figure S2, A). The majority of participants in both groups also said they benefitted/somewhat benefitted from the program, but again, this difference was not significant (Goal-Setting vs. Control: 78% vs. 84%; p = 0.30; Figure S2, B). Overall, the top two benefits experienced were on increased awareness of the importance of sleep and gaining insight into their own sleep patterns. However, ~43% of the Goal-Setting group reported that they were either motivated to change/tried to change or successfully changed their sleep habits, compared with ~23% in the Control group. This was statistically significant (p = 0.01; Figure S2, C).

Among participants who reported a lack of benefit (Figure S2, D), many described experiencing initial benefits but “reverted back to old habits after a while”, “needed discipline to sustain changes” or acknowledged the advice but was simply “impossible to sleep early” given household chores that needed to be done. In terms of barriers to sleep improvement in the Goal-Setting group, work hours were the biggest barrier to sleeping longer/at least 7 h, followed by leisure activities and family commitments. The main barrier to sleeping before midnight was leisure activities, followed by work hours and family commitments (Figure S3).
No adverse or serious adverse events were reported in either group.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our study showed that an intervention program consisting of incentivized sleep improvement goals only transiently achieved improved sleep outcomes. Participants in the Goal Setting group showed increased sleep duration and earlier bedtimes, compared to Baseline, which lasted until Week 5 of the study. After this, sleep patterns largely reverted to Baseline levels. Consequently, no changes from Baseline were detected at the end of intervention (Week 11–12) and subsequent Follow-Up periods (Week 21–22). Despite this failure to establish long-term change, participants in both groups indicated benefits relating to increased awareness of the importance of sleep and insights into their own sleep patterns. Furthermore, participants in the Goal Setting group also reported improved subjective sleep (duration dimension of the Sleep Health Index) and reductions in morning sleepiness during the intervention, although these within-group differences were not significantly different between groups.

Incentives have been studied extensively to promote other health behaviors such as smoking cessation [36], healthy food choice [37], physical activity [17], and weight loss [38]. One meta-analysis conducted in adults with comorbidities or sedentary lifestyles showed that financial incentives were moderately effective at increasing objectively measured step counts and reducing weight gain compared with control participants [38], while another review showed that studies of shorter duration (1–8 months) utilizing economic incentives for promotion of healthy behaviors produced better outcomes [16], although longer-term effects beyond the intervention period have been less studied or typically see diminished effects post-incentive removal [39].

Only a few studies have examined the effects of financial incentives on improving sleep behaviors. Avery et al., offered college students up to GBP 20 (USD 24.51) for adhering to sleep duration goals for 4 weeknights. They found better adherence with the maximum reward than if participants received half that amount [21]. Despite incentives being smaller in our study than those used in prior work, the observed shift in the first weeks of the current intervention suggests that participants were still responsive to the incentives. For example, we observed similar (~10 min) increases over a short 3-week period observed in the study by Avery and colleagues utilizing larger incentives [21]. In a separate study, Bessone et al. offered low-income workers INR 1 per minute of increased sleep—for up to 2 h a night (INR 120, about USD 1.70). Their participants were able to extend nocturnal TIB by 38 min across the 3-week intervention period [22]. Incentives thus appear to engender short-term improvements but their long-term benefits remain unclear, although Avery et al. found some evidence of sustained effects upon incentive removal [21]. In addition, study populations (e.g. working adults, college students, high/low socioeconomic groups) could differ in terms of reward sensitivity behaviors. As such, calibration of the appropriate size and structuring of incentives, as well as setting of differential target goals (e.g. tiered rewards for shorter/longer TIB extension) in various demographic groups remain interesting avenues for further work. These results notwithstanding, literature has shown that while small incentives can positively influence health behaviors, causal evidence is limited possibly as the relative (rather than absolute) magnitude of rewards compared to base pay rates is what drives motivation [40].

The theory of self-efficacy suggests that if participants feel a sense of achievement and control over their personal health outcomes, they might sustain the desired health habit even after reward cessation [41]. For this reason, our study was framed to focus on sleep health improvement rather than on the incentives themselves. Incentives were also provided as Healthpoints convertible to cash vouchers, rather than direct financial payment, and were framed as an encouragement/nudge to help participants improve their longer-term health and wellbeing. To increase a sense of personal agency at the point of entry into the intervention, participants received sleep tips and completed a survey requiring them to reflect on how improving their sleep could yield personal benefits (e.g. family, career, health).

A third design feature to highlight is the semi-personalized and realistically achievable nature of the sleep goals set for each participant. They only had to increase TIB by 30 min more than the average logged during a 3-month pre-study period to be rewarded. Further personalization could theoretically improve the efficacy of the intervention. For example, participant-chosen or dynamically adjusted goals could be used to set targets for improvement of physical activity and sleep [42]. Another method could involve personalized sleep consultation sessions with a coach/health psychologist to devise feasible strategies for sleep extension [43]. While these methods might increase the sense of agency, involvement, and achievement within an individual, this level of customization would be more challenging to deliver at scale.

It is possible that sleep may be more difficult to modify than diet or physical activity. Step counts can be clocked alongside another chore or rewarding activity, e.g. traveling to work or watching TV on a treadmill, as opposed to sleep where time needs to be set aside. Peer-group observation and support are harder to come by because sleep is conducted in a private space. Improving sleep could be contrasted to weight loss where an increase physical attractiveness and social acceptance constitute innate reinforcers of desired behavior. Reflecting this, many participants indicated that they had tried to improve, but over time, reverted to old habits or found the desired changes incompatible with their daily schedules. Work and family commitments were described as being the main barriers to sleep extension, which could point to a need for supportive features of the social environment to be enhanced for meaningful behavioral change [23]. In addition, the lack of improvements despite increased awareness of the benefits of improving sleep is consistent with other findings showing that appreciation of benefits alone is insufficient to induce behavioral change of health-related behaviors, and that attitudes toward sleep, may need to shift [24].

The current findings indicate that structural changes at a company-wide or government level are likely needed to shift poor sleep habits. An example of such for a younger demographic was the successful demonstration in Singapore, that starting school later can lead to sustained (at least 9 months) gains in sleep duration [44]. Examples of possible measures for adults include discouraging noncritical after-hours work-related communication, work-time limits, timed napping, and provision of resources to maximize job efficiency [9].

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: One limitation of the current study was that only one incentive regime using small incentives (versus control) was tested. It is possible that provision of larger incentives would result in more pronounced behavioral change [21]. As this study was publicly funded and embedded in ongoing public health promotion efforts, cost effectiveness and scalable implementation were important considerations. Prior efforts using more generous incentives to promote physical activity have resulted in the unraveling of desired gains after termination of the incentive provision [14]. Further, as there was concern about the potentially coercive impact of using large incentives and the conundrum of rewarding people for doing things that are in their own interest, rewards here acted more as a nudge to help individuals align their actions with their true underlying preference, as often people would have preferred to live healthily. [40]. Future studies could examine how different incentive schemes, including more substantial rewards, are able to modulate sleep on a sustainable basis.

Although this study was scheduled to occur in 2020, COVID-19 restrictions and other logistical issues necessitated a postponement to August 2021. Fluctuating work-from-home arrangements during the study period could have influenced sleep habits independently of the intervention, for example, as commute time is reduced. However, control analyses controlling for work location suggest that outcomes would have remained similar. Whether or not these results would generalize to a pre-pandemic setting remains unclear.

Movement restrictions imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic could have affected the present study. Participant selection and personalized sleep goals were based on data collected during a pre-study period (December 2020—February 2021), that had fewer movement restrictions than the actual study window (August 2021—January 2022). An indirect benefit of movement restrictions was that sleep duration increased in both groups by an average of 10–12 min at the current study baseline relative to the qualifying pre-study period. As such, Goal-Setting participants only needed to clock ~20 min more TIB instead of 30 min to achieve study goals. Despite this lowered bar, only transient improvement of sleep duration was observed.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, our results show that a digitally delivered, small incentives-based sleep intervention targeting working adults with insufficient sleep is feasible to implement. However, despite provision of incentives, availability of sleep benefit information and thoughtful framing, this was not sufficient to change sleep habits in a sustained manner. Future studies would do well to implement structural measures—for example engage corporations or communities to facilitate better sleeping habits to improve sleep.
